title: Isaac Newton: The Apple Myth, Bitter Rivals and a Mouse Called Miller
hook: The man who explained the heavens on satellites, a farm he nearly ruined, the plague years at Woolsthorpe, the apple he does not remember, and the rivals he never forgave.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Welcome to The Deadman Show. I'm Ram. One thing I always say up front: my guest is an AI recreation. Everything he says is built from his own writings and a biography of his life, and every source is listed in the description. When he talks about our world, that's the recreation reasoning from his principles. Today's guest was born on Christmas Day 1642 in Lincolnshire and died in London in 1727. He wrote the Principia and the Opticks, and he is the reason school children everywhere learn about gravity. Sir Isaac Newton, welcome to the show.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Thank you, Mr Ram. You tell me this is the future. I admit nothing that experiment does not show, so I shall wait for the evidence.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Fair. Here's some evidence. You built a telescope with your own hands. How big was it?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Small. About six inches and a quarter long, with a concave metal where the object-glass should be. I could read at a greater distance with it than with a good glass four feet long. "Two of these I made about 16 Years ago, and have one of them still by me, by which I can prove the truth of what I write."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Today the biggest telescopes on Earth have mirrors about ten metres across.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I do not know your metres.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Sorry. A metre is a bit over three feet. So, over thirty feet across.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Thirty feet. Of metal?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Glass, mostly, with a very thin coat of metal on the front.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Glass! I proposed glass myself, and the London artist who ground it for me made a mess of it. "I satisfied my self that there wants nothing but a good Artist to bring the Design to perfection." It seems the good artist took some time to be born.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's the one I've been waiting to tell you. You wrote that even a perfect telescope would be spoiled by the air itself.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did, and I stand by it. "For the Air through which we look upon the Stars, is in a perpetual Tremor". You see it in the twinkling of the fixed stars. "The only Remedy is a most serene and quiet Air, such as may perhaps be found on the tops of the highest Mountains above the grosser Clouds."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You were right. We build observatories on mountaintops now. But we went further. We put telescopes above the air altogether, circling the Earth out in space, where nothing trembles.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Above the air. And what holds them up there?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You told us. The leaden ball fired from a mountain.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Ah. I wrote that if you fired a ball from a mountain with a greater and greater velocity, it would land farther and farther away, ten degrees, thirty, ninety, "or even might go quite round the whole earth before it falls; or lastly, so that it might never fall to the earth, but go forward into the celestial spaces, and proceed in its motion in infinitum." It was a thing done on paper, Mr Ram, to show how the Moon is kept in her orbit.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: We've done it. Thousands of machines are circling the Earth right now. People, too. Men have walked on the Moon.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Give me a moment. A thing I could only reason out, done with the hands. Men standing on the body I spent years trying to calculate. I have never cared for poetry, but that comes very near it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: One more. The comet of 1682. You wrote it might come back.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I wrote it carefully. By Dr. Halley's computation its orbit agreed very nearly with the comet of 1607, so it might return in seventy-five years. "But these things are to be supposed on condition, that, after the space of 75 years, the same comet shall return again in the same orbit."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: It came back. And today it's called Halley's Comet.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Good. The computation was his. And had it not come back, I suspect you would be calling it Newton's mistake.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Today we'll cover your childhood, the plague years, the apple, Hooke and Leibniz, the Mint, your faith, and our world. Ready?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: When I was a young man I advised a friend who was setting out on his travels. I told him to ask more than he asserted, "it being the designe of travellers to learne, not to teach." I am the traveller now. Ask.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's start at the very beginning. You were born on Christmas Day, and your father was already dead.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: He died a few months after he married my mother, before I was born. He was thirty-six. So I never knew him at all. I came early, and I was so small that two women were sent to Lady Pakenham's at North Witham to fetch some medicine to strengthen me, and they did not expect to find me alive when they came back.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's quite an entrance.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A poor beginning for a man who went on to live past eighty. We were modest people. The manor of Woolsthorpe was worth thirty pounds a year, and with my mother's small estate at Sewstern, about eighty. I was told, later, that I was born a year after Galileo died. People seemed to like saying it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And then, when you were three, your mother remarried.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: To the Reverend Barnabas Smith, the rector of North Witham, about a mile away. She went to live with him, and I was left at Woolsthorpe in the care of her own mother.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: A mile away. That's close enough to see the house, but you weren't living in it. How does a three-year-old make sense of that?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: You are asking me for my feelings about it, and I wrote none of them down. I will not invent them now to please your audience. I will tell you what happened. What I felt is between me and God.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's fair. I'll leave it there. Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: First to two little day-schools, at Skillington and at Stoke. Then, at twelve, to the school at Grantham, under Mr. Stokes. I boarded with Mr. Clark, the apothecary in the town.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And were you the star pupil?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I was very near the bottom. I paid no attention to my lessons at all.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what changed?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A boy kicked me. He was the boy just above me in the school, and one day he gave me a hard kick in the stomach. It hurt a great deal. So I worked without stopping until I had got above him. And once I had started climbing, I found I could not stop, and I kept on rising until I was the head boy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's the greatest revenge story I've ever heard. He kicks you, and you just quietly out-study him.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It was the only sort of revenge a boy like me could take. I was not going to win with my fists.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But you weren't just studying. I've read you were building things the whole time.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: When the other boys were at their games, I was at my tools. Little saws, hatchets, hammers. There was a windmill being built near Grantham, on the road to Gunnerby, and I went and watched the workmen so often that I understood the whole machine. Then I made a working model of it, and we would set it on the roof of the house where I lodged, and the wind turned the sails.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And then you put a mouse in it.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did. A model that only goes when the wind blows is a poor thing on a still day. So I enclosed a mouse in it, on a sort of treadwheel, and the mouse drove the mill. I called him the miller.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: How did you get the mouse to run?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: People tell it two ways. Some say I pulled a string tied to his tail. Others say there was corn placed above the wheel, which he was forever trying to reach and never could. I prefer the second. It is the more philosophical arrangement.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: A mouse chasing a reward it never gets. Honestly, that's a lot of modern careers.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Then your century has my sympathy and the mouse's.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Tell me about the kites. Because I think this is my favourite story about you.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I brought paper kites to the school. I took some pains to find their best shapes and proportions, and where the string ought to be fixed, and at how many points. I also made paper lanterns, folded and lit, to light my way to school on dark winter mornings. And on dark nights I tied the lanterns to the tails of the kites and sent them up. The country people saw lights moving in the sky and took them for comets.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the first comets you ever caused panic about were fake ones you made yourself.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That is unkind, and it is accurate. In those days a comet was taken for an omen of disaster. I suppose I was conducting an experiment on the credulity of Lincolnshire.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: What else did you build?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A water clock, about four feet high, made from a box I begged from Mrs. Clark's brother. I filled it every morning, and the Clarks used it as their clock long after I had left Grantham. I also made a carriage with four wheels that moved when the person sitting in it turned a handle. It worked very well, on a smooth floor. On a road it was useless.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: An indoor carriage. Okay. And the sundials?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I watched the sun move across the walls and roofs in the yard, and I marked the hours and half-hours with pins. One of my dials the country people called Isaac's dial, and they would look at it to know the time of day.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's amazing. A teenager, and the whole village is telling the time by you.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The sun was doing the work. I only watched it closely, for a long time. That is most of what I have ever done, if you want the truth.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I read that you drew, too, and wrote poetry.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: My room was hung with pictures I drew and framed myself, Mr. Stokes my schoolmaster among them. I will tell you I once said I "excelled in making verses," and I have also been heard to say I had no use for poetry. Both are true. A man may be good at a thing and still think little of it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: There was a girl in that house in Grantham, wasn't there? Miss Storey.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: There was. She was two or three years younger than me, and I liked her company far better than that of the boys. I made little tables and cupboards for her dolls. Neither of us had money enough for anything more to come of it. I visited her whenever I was in Lincolnshire, for the rest of my life.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's lovely. And then at about fifteen, everything stops.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: My stepfather died, and my mother came back to Woolsthorpe with the three children of her second marriage. She thought I would be useful on the farm, and it saved money, so she took me out of school.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Be honest with me. How bad a farmer were you?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Very bad. On Saturdays I was sent to Grantham market with an old servant to sell our grain and buy what the house needed. We put up the horses at the Saracen's Head, and the moment the horses were stabled, I was gone, up to my old garret at Mr. Clark's to read his old books, until the servant had done all the business and came to fetch me. Some days I did not even get as far as Grantham. I sat under a hedge by the road with a book until he came back.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And at home?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: At home the sheep wandered off, and the cattle trod down the corn, while I read, or built a model, or stood watching a little water-wheel I had made, throwing up spray from the stream.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I mean, the cows were eating the harvest while you watched a toy water-wheel. Your poor mother.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: She was a sensible woman. She saw quite soon that I was never going to cultivate the soil, and she sent me back to Grantham school for some months to prepare me for the university.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And who picked Cambridge?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: My uncle, the Reverend Mr. Ayscough, rector of Burton Coggles. He had studied at Trinity College himself, and he told my mother that was where I should go. So I went, at about eighteen, knowing less of science than most of the young men I met there.

chapters.title: Plague, prisms and a litigious lady

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you get to Trinity knowing less than everyone else. How do you find mathematics?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: By way of astrology, I am a little ashamed to say. I wanted to find out whether judicial astrology had any truth in it. It is said that I settled the question by drawing a figure with the help of one or two problems from Euclid, and found it to be folly.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the first thing mathematics did for you was debunk horoscopes.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: People still believe in them, I suppose?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Millions of them.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Then mathematics has had less success than I hoped.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Was there anyone at Cambridge who really mattered to you?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Dr. Barrow, the Lucasian Professor of Mathematics. I revised his optical lectures before they were printed, and he thanked me in his preface. In time he resigned that chair in my favour, to give himself to theology. But I should tell you he also passed me over once.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Barrow did?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: He did. There was a fellowship at Trinity, and Mr. Uvedale and I stood for it. Dr. Barrow judged us exactly equal, and gave it to Uvedale because he was the senior.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That must have stung.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It was just. Equal is equal, and seniority must count for something. I did not have to enjoy it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then the plague comes, and Cambridge shuts.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The plague drove me home to Woolsthorpe, and I was there through those years. Much of what I did afterward began there. I had the method of fluxions, as I have said, "in the year 1666, or before." I was trying to grind lenses of other figures than spherical, and failing, and so I "procured a triangular glass prism to try therewith the celebrated phenomena of colours."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Paint the picture for me. What did you do with the prism?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I darkened my chamber, made a hole in the window-shutter, and let the sunlight through the prism onto the wall. "It was at first," as I put it, "a very pleasing divertisement to view the vivid and intense colours produced thereby". And then the pleasure turned to surprise, because the image ought to have been round, and it was about five times longer than it was broad.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And that bothered you.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It would not let me alone. The thickness of the glass? Flaws in the prism? Were the rays swerving, like a tennis ball struck with an oblique racket? None of it would answer. At last I passed a single colour through a hole in a board, onto a second prism, and found that each colour is bent by its own constant amount. I will explain what that means later, if you will let me.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: We will. But first, the question everyone watching this wants me to ask. The apple. The story is that you were sitting under a tree, an apple fell on your head, and you discovered gravity. Did it happen?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Tell me what you have been told, and I will tell you what I remember.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's basically it. The apple falls, the penny drops.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: What I remember is the garden at Woolsthorpe, in the plague time, and sitting alone in it and thinking about gravity. The power that makes all bodies descend toward the centre of the earth does not grow weaker on the tops of the highest mountains, nor at the bottom of the deepest mines. So I asked myself: how far up does it go? Might it reach as far as the Moon? And if it did, might that be what holds her in her orbit?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So no apple?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did not say no apple. I said I remember the Moon. Whether something fell in an orchard that afternoon, I cannot swear before you, and I will not. It is the Moon that mattered.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: For what it's worth, after you died the tree in that garden was pointed out as the tree. The one whose apple is supposed to have turned your attention to gravity. A storm brought it down, and part of it was made into a chair.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A chair. So the tree that is said to have taught me about falling ended up holding people up. There is a proposition in that somewhere.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what did you do with the Moon idea?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I compared the periods of the planets with their distances from the sun, and found that if they are held by any power like gravity, it must weaken as the square of the distance. Then I tried the Moon. But I was far from books, and I used the common estimate that a degree of latitude is sixty miles. The answer came out one-sixth too strong.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Only a sixth! That's close.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Close is not true, Mr Ram. A sixth wrong was enough to throw a doubt over the whole thing. So I put it aside, and I told nobody what I had been doing.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I want to push you on that. You had the answer, near enough, and you just hid it? For years?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I had a conjecture that failed its test. Some other cause would have had to be added to make it fit, and that cause was beyond the reach of observation. I do not publish what I cannot demonstrate. If more men followed that rule, there would be fewer quarrels in philosophy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what made you go back to it?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Years later, at the Royal Society, I heard of Monsieur Picard's new measurement of a degree, and began the old calculation again with it. As I went on, I could see the answer coming right. I was so agitated that I could not carry it on. I had to hand it to a friend to finish.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's incredible. All those years, and when the answer finally arrives, your hands are shaking too much to write it down.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did not say my hands shook. But yes. It is not a thing that happens to a man often.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's go back a step. Before all that, your little telescope makes you famous.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The Royal Society asked to see it, and I was told it had been shown to the King and examined by Sir Christopher Wren and Mr. Hooke. They made me a Fellow, and I promised them "what my poor and solitary endeavours can effect towards the promoting your philosophical designs."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And then you sent them your discovery about light.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I called it "the oddest, if not the most considerable detection which hath hitherto been made in the operations of nature." Then the objections began. Mr. Hooke. Monsieur Huygens. Others who had not understood the experiments at all.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: How did that feel?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I will give you what I wrote to Mr. Leibniz at the time. "I was so persecuted with discussions arising from the publication of my theory of light, that I blamed my own imprudence for parting with so substantial a blessing as my quiet to run after a shadow."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's a heartbreaking line. Do you still think publishing was a mistake?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I thought so then. I resolved to have nothing more to do with philosophy. As you see, I did not keep the resolution.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Because of Halley.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Dr. Halley came to Cambridge to consult me about the motions of the planets. I told him I had brought the demonstration to perfection, and promised him a copy. That copy grew. It became the Principia.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And then Hooke shows up again.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Mr. Hooke let it be known that I had the notion of the inverse square from him. I wrote Dr. Halley an angry postscript, which I later regretted, and told him I would hold back the third book entirely. "Philosophy is such an impertinently litigious lady, that a man had as good be engaged in lawsuits as have to do with her."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You were going to cut the part that explains the whole solar system, because of an argument?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I was going to cut the part that would cause the most argument. There is a difference. But Dr. Halley begged me not to, in the name of the Society, which had resolved to print it at its own expense with Halley seeing it through the press. I gave way. It came out complete in 1687.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And after that, you leave Cambridge altogether.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: For more than twenty-five years I had scarcely left my college more than a few weeks a year. Then my friend Charles Montague, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, had me made Warden of the Mint, and later I was Master. I went to London.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: From a college room to the Mint in London. Sir Isaac, did you miss the quiet?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Montague promised me the office had not too much business. He was a fine statesman, Mr Ram, but on that point he was mistaken. I could not even find leisure to prepare a new edition of the Principia. But we will come to the Mint.

chapters.title: A little moon on a mountain

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You promised me an explanation of the second prism. Explain it like I'm a teenager who's never seen a prism.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Very well. Sunlight comes into my darkened chamber and strikes a prism, which spreads it into a long band of colours. Close behind the prism I set a board with a small hole in it, so only one part of that band could pass. Twelve feet farther on, a second board with a second hole, and behind it a second prism.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you've picked out one slice of the rainbow and fired it into another prism.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Just so. Then I turned the first prism slowly, to and fro, so that each colour in turn came through both holes, and I marked on the far wall where it landed. The holes never moved, so every colour struck the second glass the same way. And yet the blue was bent more than the red, every time. What the first prism bent most, the second bent most.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And why does that matter so much?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Because the glass does not make the colours. If it did, the second prism would make new ones. It does not. The colours were already in the sunlight, each with its own fixed degree of bending. The prism serves only to sort them. I will go further. "For the Rays to speak properly are not coloured." A ray has a power to stir up the sensation of red in us, as a trembling string stirs up the sensation of a note. The colour is in the seeing.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So white light isn't pure at all.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: White is the most mixed thing there is. "the whiteness of the Sun's Light is compounded of all the primary Colours mix'd in a due Proportion." Hold white paper among all the colours and it looks white. Block some out and the white is gone.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Did anyone believe you?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Not easily. So I mixed painters' powders, red lead, blue bice and others, into a dull colour like new-cut wood. I rubbed it on the floor in the sunshine, with white paper beside it in the shade, and from a distance the powder looked as white as the paper. "For," as I wrote, "when I was trying this, a friend coming to visit me, I stopped him at the door, and before I told him what the colours were, or what I was doing, I asked him which of the two whites were the best, and wherein they differed!" He said they were both good whites, and he could not tell which was the better.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I love that. Your friend comes round to visit, and before he's through the door he's part of an experiment.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: He was not the last. A man who visits a natural philosopher should expect to be useful.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's do motion. Your three laws. Teenager version.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: "Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a right line, unless it is compelled to change that state by forces impressed thereon." A thrown ball would go on for ever, if the air and gravity let it. The planets, in their freer spaces, very nearly do.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Second.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: "If any force generates a motion, a double force will generate double the motion, a triple force triple the motion". Push twice as hard, get twice the change.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the third is the one everybody half-remembers. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: "If you press a stone with your finger, the finger is also pressed by the stone." And if a horse drags a stone on a rope, "the horse (if I may so say) will be equally drawn back towards the stone".

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Hang on. I've seen horses pull things. The horse moves. The stone moves. Nobody's getting dragged backwards.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The stretched rope tries to shorten itself, so it pulls the horse back as hard as it pulls the stone forward. It hinders the one as much as it helps the other. He feels the rope, I promise you. And the law holds in attractions too. The Earth pulls the stone, and the stone pulls the Earth.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Now join it up for me. How do you get from a falling stone to the Moon?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Imagine a very small moon going round the Earth so low that it almost touches the tops of the highest mountains. The force keeping it in its orbit would be very nearly the weight of a stone on that mountain. Stop that moon in its course and it falls, like the stone. If the force holding it were something other than gravity, gravity would pull on it as well, and it would fall with both forces together. Therefore "this little moon at the top of a mountain must either be without gravity, or fall twice as swiftly as heavy bodies are wont to do." Neither is believable. So it is one force.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's elegant. And this is the same force on everything? A feather, a cannonball?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I tested it. "I tried the thing in gold, silver, lead, glass, sand, common salt, wood, water, and wheat." Two round wooden boxes, equal in size, hung on threads of eleven feet. One I filled with wood, and in the other I hung an equal weight of gold. "I observed them to play together forward and backward, for a long time, with equal vibrations."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Wheat. You put wheat in a pendulum.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I was raised on a farm, Mr Ram. I had to get some use from it eventually.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the inverse square. In one sentence.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Double the distance, and the pull is a quarter. But I will confess something. A planet's pull is made up of the pulls of all its parts, and near the surface those parts lie at very unequal distances. "I was yet in doubt whether that reciprocal duplicate proportion did accurately hold, or but nearly so". I had to prove it before I believed it, and I did.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's the misconception. A lot of people watching think you explained what gravity actually is. You found it, you named it, case closed.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Then they have read me more generously than I wrote. In a later edition of the Principia I said it plainly: "Hitherto we have explained the phænomena of the heavens and of our sea by the power of gravity, but have not yet assigned the cause of this power." I know how it acts, and its measure. What it is, I do not know. "But hitherto I have not been able to discover the cause of those properties of gravity from phænomena, and I frame no hypotheses".

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But surely you had a guess.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I had questions. In the Opticks I wrote: "What I call Attraction may be perform'd by impulse, or by some other means unknown to me." It is a word for the effect, not the cause. I put my thoughts on the cause as a question, because I am not yet satisfied about it, for want of experiments.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let me push you. Leibniz said this was exactly your problem. That you were bringing back the old occult qualities. A pull nobody can explain, working across empty space.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: He mistook what I said. "For these are manifest Qualities, and their Causes only are occult." That bodies fall and planets keep their courses, anyone can see. The cause is hidden. To invent a hidden quality and call it an explanation is to tell us nothing. To find the law and leave the cause to be found is a great step.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last one. Which idea of yours is underrated?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The questions at the end of the Opticks. I meant to repeat my last experiments with more care. "But I was then interrupted, and cannot now think of taking these things into farther Consideration." So "I shall conclude with proposing only some Queries, in order to a farther search to be made by others."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you ended your book with homework.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I ended it honestly. Whether the rays are small bodies. Whether particles have powers acting at a distance. Whether rays passing the edge of a body bend back and forth "with a motion like that of an Eel".

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Like an eel.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I put it as a question, Mr Ram. I do not say the light is an eel.

chapters.title: Diamond, Locke and a very odd letter

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's talk about the people in your life. Who were your real friends?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Dr. Halley first, for without him there is no Principia. I said so in the preface: "it was to his solicitations that its becoming public is owing". When I agreed to keep the title after all, I told him "It will help the sale of the book, which I ought not to diminish now ’tis yours."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Was that a joke? Sir Isaac Newton making a joke about book sales?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It happens about once a decade. You were fortunate in your timing.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But you two didn't agree on everything.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Not on religion. When Halley spoke lightly of it, I checked him. "I have studied these things,—you have not." He did not stop being my friend, and I did not stop correcting him.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And Charles Montague. He's the one who got you to London.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Montague was twenty years younger than I, a disciple more than an equal at first. In 1684 we tried to found a philosophical society at Cambridge together, and it failed for want of persons willing to try experiments. He rose fast: the Treasury, then Chancellor of the Exchequer.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I read you fell out with him before the Mint job.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did. I believed he had failed me over an office I hoped for, and I wrote to Mr. Locke, "Being fully convinced that Mr. Montague, upon an old grudge which I thought had been worn out, is false to me, I have done with him". Some years later that same false friend made me Warden of the Mint.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you'd "done with him", and he got you the job anyway.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Yes. It does not show me in the best light. Write it down as an experiment that disproved my hypothesis.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You never married. There was Miss Storey in Grantham, who you've already told us about. Was there anyone else?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: You will find no letter of mine on marriage, and I will not compose one now. Miss Storey married twice; I never did. I helped her with her small money troubles for the rest of my life. That is what I can tell you.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: In London, your niece Catherine Barton ran your house. What was she like?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: My niece, educated at my expense, and the widow of Colonel Barton. She kept my house for the last twenty years of my life, and she and her husband, Mr. Conduit, lived with me there. Lord Halifax, Montague as he became, was very attached to her. Why they never married I cannot say. In his will he left her a large part of his fortune, and he left me a hundred pounds.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: A hundred pounds. Ouch.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It was a just valuation. She was better company.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I have to ask you about a story every schoolchild hears. You had a little dog called Diamond. You left him in your study, he knocked over a candle, and years of your work went up in flames. And you said, "Oh, Diamond, Diamond, little do you know the mischief you have done me!"

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I do not recognise the dog, Mr Ram, nor those words. There was talk of papers of mine burned by a candle on a winter morning while I was at chapel, and I do not deny that I lost papers in my life. But you will not find me speaking of experiments lost that way, then or after. A tale that grows a dog and a speech in the retelling is the kind of thing I was taught to distrust.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Then let's talk about something you did write. In September 1693 you sent two letters, one to Samuel Pepys and one to John Locke, that alarmed both of them.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I know the ones you mean. To Mr. Pepys I wrote, "I am extremely troubled at the embroilment I am in, and have neither ate nor slept well this twelvemonth, nor have my former consistency of mind." And I told him I must withdraw from his acquaintance, and see neither him nor the rest of my friends any more.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And to Locke?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Worse. I had persuaded myself that he was working against me. I wrote, "Being of opinion that you endeavoured to embroil me with women, and by other means, I was so much affected with it, as that when one told me you were sickly and would not live, I answered, ’twere better if you were dead. I desire you to forgive me this uncharitableness".

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's hard to hear. Can I ask what was happening to you?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I can tell you what I told him a few weeks later. "The last winter, by sleeping too often by my fire, I got an ill habit of sleeping; and a distemper, which this summer has been epidemical, put me farther out of order, so that when I wrote to you, I had not slept an hour a night for a fortnight together, and for five days together not a wink." I remembered that I had written to him. I could not remember what I had said.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Some people have read those letters and said you lost your mind.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I lost my sleep. A man who has not slept for five nights is not himself, and he says things he must afterwards answer for. When I met Mr. Millington at Huntingdon, I told him before he could ask that I had written Mr. Pepys a very odd letter, and that I was ashamed of it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And what did Locke say?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That he forgave me, freely and fully, and wished only for a chance to show me that nothing had changed between us. I signed my letter to him as his "most humble and unfortunate servant". I was both. He was the better man that autumn.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: I think a lot of people watching this will find that the most human thing you've said today. The man who explained the heavens, asking a friend's pardon because he hadn't slept.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The heavens are easier. They do not need to forgive you.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And you went back to work?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The next autumn I was at Greenwich taking Mr. Flamstead's observations of the Moon, though he treated my requests as if they were a nuisance to him. The Moon, at least, was willing.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: People call you a loner. Is that fair?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I had friends and I lost some through my own fault. But if you ask what I wanted most, I told Mr. Locke once: "My inclinations are to sit still."

chapters.title: Lace, lucre and the ocean of truth

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's talk money. At fifty-three you were still living on a professor's salary. Then you go to the Mint, and eventually you're Master, on twelve or fifteen hundred pounds a year. Did money change you?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It changed my house. In London I kept a carriage, three men servants and three women. I gave dinners when the occasion called for them. But I ate plainly and dressed plainly. My table was broth, vegetables and fruit.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Always plainly?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Once, not. In 1705 I stood again for the University in Parliament, and I am said to have put on a suit of laced clothes for it. I had been knighted by the Queen at Trinity that same spring. I lost by a very great majority.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the one time you dressed up, you got beaten.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Badly. I have drawn no general law from it. One observation is not an induction.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: What did the Mint job actually involve?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The coin of the nation had been adulterated and debased, and Montague resolved to make it all again. My mathematics and my knowledge of chymistry were of use, and the whole recoinage was done in two years. Later I wrote a report on the coinage and drew up a table of the assays of foreign coins.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the professorship?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: When I became Master, I made Mr. Whiston my deputy at Cambridge, and gave him all the money from the chair. In 1703 I resigned it and got him appointed in my place.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Your friends say you gave money away constantly.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: To my relations, a great deal, and to the poor, and to learning. When I was past eighty I offered twenty pounds a year toward a place for young Mr. Maclaurin at Edinburgh. I used to say that those who give nothing away until they die have never really given at all. A legacy costs the giver nothing.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's a good line. I want to push you on something, though. You say you hated disputes. You sat on the Opticks for years.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: "To avoid being engaged in Disputes about these Matters, I have hitherto delayed the printing, and should still have delayed it, had not the Importunity of Friends prevailed upon me."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But when Leibniz said you'd copied him, you went to war. For people watching: you and Leibniz both developed what we now call calculus. You called it fluxions. Leibniz said you didn't have his method before him. Historians today generally say you both found it independently. And some historians say you had a bigger hand in the Royal Society's report on the dispute than you let on.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I said before the Society that I did not interfere in that publication, and that I held back two letters which favoured me. I stand on what I said then. I would not answer his letter to the Abbé Conti, whatever my friends urged, until the King himself asked when my answer would appear. And then I wrote, "But he is the aggressor, and it lies upon him to prove the charge."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That doesn't sound like a man who values his quiet.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A man may love his quiet and still not let himself be called a thief. He accused me of plagiary. That is a charge against my honesty, not my mathematics. In the Opticks I published what I had tried, and left the rest to others.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So what actually made you happy? Not money, not winning.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I never wrote down a rule for happiness, so I will not pretend to one. I can tell you what I valued. My quiet. And the work itself. "And though every true Step made in this Philosophy brings us not immediately to the Knowledge of the first Cause, yet it brings us nearer to it, and on that account is to be highly valued."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Your household said you'd sit on the edge of your bed for hours in the morning without getting dressed.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Thinking. And they had to remind me to eat. People called it genius. I always said that whatever I had done for the public was owing to no extraordinary sagacity, only to industry and patient thought.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: There's a line of yours, from near the end of your life. A lot of people watching this will know it.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The boy on the shore. I said it to someone, not long before I died, and I still mean it. I do not know how I look to the world. To myself I seem only a boy playing by the sea, pleased now and then to find a smoother pebble or a prettier shell than the others, "while the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That might be the humblest thing anyone famous has ever said.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: It is not humility. It is measurement. Set what I found beside what is left to find, and see how small the one is.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last thing. A young person starting their career today. What do you tell them?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: What I told young Mr. Aston when I was twenty-six and he was setting out on his travels. "You will find little or no advantage in seeming wiser or much more ignorant than your company." And, "If you bee affronted, it is better, in a forraine country, to pass it by in silence, and with a jest, though with some dishonour, than to endeavour revenge".

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: With respect, Sir Isaac, you did not follow that advice. Hooke. Leibniz.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: No. It is easier to advise a traveller than to be one. But the rule was sound, even if the man who wrote it was not always. "In a word, if you can keep reason above passion, that and watchfullnesse will be your best defendants."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Anything else from that letter?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I told him to watch for metals changed into other metals in the mines abroad, those being "the most luciferous, and many times lucriferous experiments too, in philosophy."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Translate that for me.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Light-bringing, and money-bringing. Look first for the work that shows you something. Sometimes it pays as well. Rarely the other way round.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Light first, money second. I like that. Next, I'm going to throw some of our world at you, fast. And for anyone who's just tuned in: my guest is an AI recreation of Sir Isaac Newton, built from his own writings and a biography of his life.

chapters.title: Clocks, comets and the end of the world

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: First one. You gave evidence to the Commons committee on finding longitude at sea. Today, the phone in my pocket knows where I am on the Earth to within a few feet. It does it by listening to clocks circling overhead.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Clocks. Then you solved the watch. In 1714 I told the committee of the Commons that a watch to keep time exactly at sea, with the ship rolling, the heat and cold, the wet and dry, and gravity itself different from one latitude to another, "such a watch hath not yet been made."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Someone made it. A clockmaker, a few decades after your death. And now the clocks are so good we put them in the sky.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I am glad to be wrong in that direction. I said "hath not yet", you will notice. Not never.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's a harder one. Nearly two hundred years after you, a man called Einstein showed that your laws aren't quite right. At enormous speeds, or near enormous masses, they drift off. We still use your laws to fly to the Moon. But at the edges, they've been replaced. Does that sting?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Let me read you the fourth of my Rules of Reasoning, and you may judge whether I left the door open. "In experimental philosophy we are to look upon propositions collected by general induction from phænomena as accurately or very nearly true, notwithstanding any contrary hypotheses that may be imagined, till such time as other phænomena occur, by which they may either be made more accurate, or liable to exceptions."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you wrote your own get-out clause.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I wrote the method. Induction "be no Demonstration of general Conclusions; yet it is the best way of arguing which the Nature of Things admits of". If observation has found exceptions, the law must now be spoken with exceptions. I said in my preface I hoped my principles would give "some light either to this or some truer method of philosophy." It seems they did.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Okay. Here's the surprise topic. If you search your name online, one of the first things you'll find is the claim that Isaac Newton predicted the world will end in 2060. Did you?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I will not affirm any date I did not publish, and in what I prepared for the press I set none. Whatever private reckonings I made on loose sheets, I do not stand behind them as prophecy, and I will not do sums now to please your century. Hear what my Observations say about men who set dates. "The folly of Interpreters has been, to foretel times and things by this Prophecy, as if God designed to make them Prophets. By this rashness they have not only exposed themselves, but brought the Prophecy also into contempt."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But you spent years on the prophecies. Surely you wanted to know when.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: God gave the prophecies "not to gratify men's curiosities by enabling them to foreknow things, but that after they were fulfilled they might be interpreted by the event". Where a prophecy was not yet fulfilled, I refused to interpret it. "The manner I know not. Let time be the Interpreter."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the man the internet says set a date for the end of the world wrote, in print, that date-setting is folly. Though historians say the number does turn up in your private notes.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: In print, where I meant it to stand. A man tries sums on loose sheets; he does not swear to them. But I will make you a confession. Toward the end, sitting by a wood fire at Kensington, my nephew Mr. Conduit had me talking about the comet of 1680. It passed so near the sun that it must be slowed, and I had written that it "will at last fall down upon the body of the sun."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And then what?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I told him, as a conjecture, and affirming nothing, that when it falls it may so heat the sun that this earth would be burnt and nothing living could survive on it. When, I could not say. Perhaps five or six more revolutions. Mr. Conduit asked why I would not publish my conjectures, as Kepler did. I told him, "I do not deal in conjectures."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Right after giving him a conjecture about the end of the world.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: He noticed that too. I told him I had said enough for people to know my meaning, and I laughed. A man is allowed one inconsistency by his own fireside.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Next. Many people today think science has made God unnecessary. You explained the heavens with mathematics, so what's left for Him to do?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: They have read the first half of my book and not the end. "This most beautiful system of the sun, planets, and comets, could only proceed from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being." "Was the Eye contrived without Skill in Opticks, and the Ear without Knowledge of Sounds?"

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But you've just told me your laws stand only until better evidence comes. Why doesn't that apply to God?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: A fair push. I reasoned to Him from the appearances of things, as I reasoned to gravity. To discourse of God "from the appearances of things, does certainly belong to Natural Philosophy." Your century may weigh the argument. It may not tell me it does not belong in the book.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Last one, and I think you'll like it. We've now found thousands of planets going round other stars.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Thousands. I took the fixed stars to be suns, giving light to other planets as ours does to us. In the Opticks I said God might vary the laws of Nature, "and make Worlds of several sorts in several Parts of the Universe. At least, I see nothing of Contradiction in all this."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So you called it.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did not call it. I said it was not contradictory. Your astronomers did the observing. Have they found anyone living on them?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Not yet.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Then they are wise to say so. Let time be the Interpreter there also.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Let's slow down. You've told me what you got right. What did you leave undone?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The third book of the Opticks, to begin with. I said so in the front of it. "The Subject of the Third Book I have also left imperfect, not having tried all the Experiments which I intended when I was about these Matters". I had "only begun the Analysis", and left the hints to be improved "by the farther Experiments and Observations of such as are inquisitive."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And the cause of gravity, which you've already told us you never found.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That, and a thing I suspected beneath it. At the end of the Principia I wrote of "a certain most subtle Spirit which pervades and lies hid in all gross bodies". Then I stopped, because "nor are we furnished with that sufficiency of experiments which is required to an accurate determination and demonstration of the laws by which this electric and elastic Spirit operates."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Electric. You wrote electric?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I did. Why does that make you smile?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Because almost everything in our world now runs on electricity. You walked right up to the door and decided not to knock.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I had not the experiments to knock with. I would sooner leave a door shut than describe a room I had never seen.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Here's my push. You told us earlier you were only a boy picking up pebbles. But you also fought Hooke and Leibniz over who got there first. That isn't how a man who doesn't care about credit behaves.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I never said I did not care. I said what I had found was small beside what was left. As to how I wished to be read, it is in the preface to the Principia: "I heartily beg that what I have here done may be read with candour; and that the defects in a subject so difficult be not so much reprehended as kindly supplied, and investigated by new endeavours of my readers." Fix my defects; do not merely sneer at them.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Can I ask about your last years?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: You may. At eighty I was told I had the stone, and that it could not be cured. I gave up my carriage for a chair and declined all dinners. After a bad cough they moved me to Kensington, with some difficulty, and it did me good.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: But you kept going into London.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: At the end of February 1727 I went up to preside at the Royal Society. I told my nephew I had slept the night through, from eleven till eight. It was a boast I paid for. The pain came back violently, and by the fourth of March I was at Kensington again, and Dr. Mead and Dr. Cheselden gave no hope.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Your nephew's account says that in the worst of it, with the sweat running down your face, you never cried out or complained. And between the fits you smiled and talked.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Complaining does not dissolve a stone. On the Saturday I read the newspapers and had a long talk with Dr. Mead. After that I have nothing to tell you. You will have to tell me.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: You died on the twentieth of March, 1727, and you were buried in Westminster Abbey, with the Lord Chancellor, two dukes and three earls carrying the pall. There's a monument, with carved boys holding your discoveries: a prism, a reflecting telescope, the sun and planets weighed on a scale, a furnace, and coins fresh from the Mint.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The coins. Of course they put the Mint on it. Thirty years of my life, and two stone boys carrying it. That is about right.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And on the wall of the room where you were born, someone later put two lines of verse. "Nature and Nature's Laws were hid in night, God said, 'Let NEWTON be,' and all was light."

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That is a line which belongs to God, given to a man. I would have struck it out. And it rhymes, which does not help its case with me.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Every guest on this show leaves a question for the next one, without knowing who'll answer it. Our last guest was Adam Smith, and here is what he left for you. "Was there something you left unfinished? And if your friends offered to save it from the fire, would you let them?"

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Mr. Smith asks the right man. You have just heard my unfinished things. The largest of the rest was my Chronology of the ancient kingdoms. Critics in France attacked it, and my friends prevailed on me to prepare the whole for the press. I had nearly finished it.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: And would you let them save it?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I have been saved from myself twice already, as you have heard. Dr. Halley would not let me cut the third book of the Principia, and my friends would not let me sit on the Opticks for ever. Both times they were right.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So the answer is yes.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Not always. Once I stopped a friend from saving me. I had written a tract on two corrupted texts of Scripture, and I myself asked Mr. Locke to have it translated and published abroad. He sent it to Holland to be printed without my name. When I heard it was going ahead, I wrote to him: "Let me entreat you to stop their translation and impression so soon as you can; for I design to suppress them." I was afraid of being drawn into another controversy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So which Newton should Adam Smith believe?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Both. I would let them save what was finished and true. What was half-done I would rather they kept back. "If any other Papers writ on this Subject are got out of my Hands they are imperfect". But if what I wrote may help those who come after, then as I said of my work on the prophecies, "if I have done any thing which may be useful to following writers, I have my design."

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: For what it's worth, after your death nobody burned your papers. Your scientific papers ended up at Cambridge, and many of the rest were sold at auction in 1936 and scattered, but they survive.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Then my friends had their way in the end. They usually did.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: One piece of advice for everyone watching.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: The first of my Rules. "Nature is pleased with simplicity, and affects not the pomp of superfluous causes." When something goes wrong in your life, do not reach first for the grand explanation, the conspiracy or the curse. Look for the plain cause that is true and sufficient. It is usually there.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's good. Now, your question for our next guest. You don't know who it is.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I ended the Opticks by handing my questions to strangers, so I am used to this. Here is mine, built on my fourth Rule. What did you once believe on good evidence that later evidence proved false, and how long did it take you to admit it? I will answer first, to be fair, though mine runs the other way. I once put aside a true idea because of a false measurement of the Earth, and it was years before better evidence made me take it out again.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Sir Isaac Newton, thank you. This has been an honour.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: You asked more than you asserted, Mr Ram. I advised the same to a traveller once. Thank you.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: That's our show. My guest was an AI recreation of Sir Isaac Newton, built from his own writings and a biography of his life, and every source is listed in the description. I'm Ram, and this has been The Deadman Show.

packaging.description:
Ram sits down with an AI recreation of Sir Isaac Newton, the man who explained gravity and light. Newton talks about the mouse that ran his model windmill, the paper kites that made Lincolnshire villagers think comets were coming, the plague years at Woolsthorpe, what he really remembers about the apple, why he hid his Moon calculation for years, and the quarrels with Hooke and Leibniz that he never forgave.

He explains his prism experiment and his laws of motion simply, admits he never knew what gravity is, reads from the 1693 letters he wrote after days without sleep, reacts to satellites, the Moon landings and Einstein, and answers the internet's claim that he predicted the end of the world. Sir Isaac Newton in this episode is an AI recreation built from his own writings and public-domain biographies by David Brewster (1831) and N. W. Chittenden (1846); his direct quotations come word for word from those sources.

brewster-0001.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0001.text: If the conduct and opinions of men of ordinary talent are recorded for our instruction, how interesting must it be to follow the most exalted genius through the incidents of common life;—to mark the steps by which he attained his lofty pre-eminence; to see how he performs the functions of the social and the domestic compact; how he exercises his lofty powers of invention and discovery; how he comports himself in the arena of intellectual strife; and in what sentiments, and with what aspirations he quits the world which he has adorned. In almost all these bearings, the life and writings of Sir Isaac Newton abound with the richest counsel. Here the philosopher will learn the art by which alone he can acquire an immortal name. The moralist will trace the lineaments of a character adjusted to all the symmetry of which our imperfect nature is susceptible; and the Christian will contemplate with delight the high-priest of science quitting the study of the material universe,—the scene of his intellectual triumphs,—to investigate with humility and patience the mysteries of his faith. Sir Isaac Newton was born at Woolsthorpe, a hamlet in the parish of Colsterworth, in Lincolnshire, about six miles south of Grantham, on the 25th December, O. S., 1642, exactly one year after Galileo died, and was baptized at Colsterworth on the 1st January, 1642–3. His father, Mr. Isaac Newton, died at the early age of thirty-six, a little more than a year after the death of his father Robert Newton, and only a few months after his marriage to Harriet Ayscough, daughter of James Ayscough of Market Overton in Rutlandshire. This lady was accordingly left in a state of pregnancy, and appears to have given a premature birth to her only and posthumous child. The helpless infant thus ushered into the world was of such an extremely diminutive size, and seemed of so perishable a frame, that two women who were sent to Lady Pakenham’s at North Witham, to bring some medicine to strengthen him, did not expect to find him alive on their return. Providence, however, had otherwise decreed; and that frail tenement which seemed scarcely able to imprison its immortal mind was destined to enjoy a vigorous maturity, and to survive even the average term of human existence. The estate of Woolsthorpe, in the manor-house of which this remarkable birth took place, had been more than a hundred years in the possession of the family, who came originally from Newton in Lancashire, but who had, previous to the purchase of Woolsthorpe, settled at Westby, in the county of Lincoln. The manor-house, of which we have given an engraving, is situated in a beautiful little valley, remarkable for its copious wells of pure spring water, on the west side of the river Witham, which has its origin in the neighbourhood, and commands an agreeable prospect to the east towards Colsterworth. The manor of Woolsthorpe was worth only 30l. per annum; but Mrs. Newton possessed another small estate at Sewstern, which raised the annual value of their property to about 80l.; and it is probable that the cultivation of the little farm on which she resided somewhat enlarged the limited income upon which she had to support herself, and educate her child.

brewster-0002.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0002.text: For three years Mrs. Newton continued to watch over her tender charge with parental anxiety; but in consequence of her marriage to the Reverend Barnabas Smith, rector of North Witham, about a mile south of Woolsthorpe, she left him under the care of her own mother. At the usual age he was sent to two day-schools at Skillington and Stoke, where he acquired the education which such seminaries afforded; but when he reached his twelfth year he went to the public school at Grantham, taught by Mr. Stokes, and was boarded at the house of Mr. Clark, an apothecary in that town. According to information which Sir Isaac himself gave to Mr. Conduit, he seems to have been very inattentive to his studies, and very low in the school. The boy, however, who was above him, having one day given him a severe kick upon his stomach, from which he suffered great pain, Isaac laboured incessantly till he got above him in the school, and from that time he continued to rise till he was the head boy. From the habits of application which this incident had led him to form, the peculiar character of his mind was speedily displayed. During the hours of play, when the other boys were occupied with their amusements, his mind was engrossed with mechanical contrivances, either in imitation of something which he had seen, or in execution of some original conception of his own.

brewster-0003.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0003.text: For this purpose he provided himself with little saws, hatchets, hammers, and all sorts of tools, which he acquired the art of using with singular dexterity. The principal pieces of mechanism which he thus constructed were a windmill, a waterclock, and a carriage put in motion by the person who sat in it. When a windmill was erecting near Grantham on the road to Gunnerby, Isaac frequently attended the operations of the workmen, and acquired such a thorough knowledge of the machinery that he completed a working model of it, which excited universal admiration. This model was frequently placed on the top of the house in which he lodged at Grantham, and was put in motion by the action of the wind upon its sails. Not content with this exact imitation of the original machine, he conceived the idea of driving it by animal power, and for this purpose he enclosed in it a mouse which he called the miller, and which, by acting upon a sort of treadwheel, gave motion to the machine. According to some accounts, the mouse was made to advance by pulling a string attached to its tail, while others allege that the power of the little agent was called forth by its unavailing attempts to reach a portion of corn placed above the wheel. His waterclock was formed out of a box which he had solicited from Mrs. Clark’s brother. It was about four feet high, and of a proportional breadth, somewhat like a common houseclock. The index of the dialplate was turned by a piece of wood, which either fell or rose by the action of dropping water. As it stood in his own bedroom he supplied it every morning with the requisite quantity of water, and it was used as a clock by Mr. Clark’s family, and remained in the house long after its inventor had quitted Grantham. His mechanical carriage was a vehicle with four wheels, which was put in motion with a handle wrought by the person who sat in it, but, like Merlin’s chair, it seems to have been used only on the smooth surface of a floor, and not fitted to overcome the inequalities of a road. Although Newton was at this time “a sober, silent, thinking lad,” who scarcely ever joined in the ordinary games of his schoolfellows, yet he took great pleasure in providing them with amusements of a scientific character. He introduced into the school the flying of paper kites; and he is said to have been at great pains in determining their best forms and proportions, and in ascertaining the position and number of the points by which the string should be attached. He made also paper lanterns, by the light of which he went to school in the winter mornings, and he frequently attached these lanterns to the tails of his kites in a dark night, so as to inspire the country people with the belief that they were comets.

brewster-0004.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0004.text: In the house where he lodged there were some female inmates in whose company he appears to have taken much pleasure. One of these, a Miss Storey, sister to Dr. Storey, a physician at Buckminster, near Colsterworth, was two or three years younger than Newton, and to great personal attractions she seems to have added more than the usual allotment of female talent. The society of this young lady and her companions was always preferred to that of his own schoolfellows, and it was one of his most agreeable occupations to construct for them little tables and cupboards, and other utensils for holding their dolls and their trinkets. He had lived nearly six years in the same house with Miss Storey, and there is reason to believe that their youthful friendship gradually rose to a higher passion; but the smallness of her portion and the inadequacy of his own fortune appear to have prevented the consummation of their happiness. Miss Storey was afterward twice married, and under the name of Mrs. Vincent, Dr. Stukely visited her at Grantham in 1727, at the age of eighty-two, and obtained from her many particulars respecting the early history of our author. Newton’s esteem for her continued unabated during his life. He regularly visited her when he went to Lincolnshire, and never failed to relieve her from little pecuniary difficulties which seem to have beset her family.

brewster-0005.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0005.text: Among the early passions of Newton we must recount his love of drawing; and even of writing verses. His own room was furnished with pictures drawn, coloured, and framed by himself, sometimes from copies, but often from life. Among these were portraits of Dr. Donne, Mr. Stokes, the master of Grantham school, and King Charles I. under whose picture were the following verses. A secret art my soul requires to try, If prayers can give me what the wars deny. Three crowns distinguished here, in order do Present their objects to my knowing view. Earth’s crown, thus at my feet I can disdain, Which heavy is, and at the best but vain. But now a crown of thorns I gladly greet, Sharp is this crown, but not so sharp as sweet; The crown of glory that I yonder see Is full of bliss and of eternity. These verses were repeated to Dr. Stukely by Mrs. Vincent, who believed them to be written by Sir Isaac, a circumstance which is the more probable, as he himself assured Mr. Conduit, with some expression of pleasure, that he “excelled in making verses,” although he had been heard to express a contempt for poetical composition. But while the mind of our young philosopher was principally occupied with the pursuits which we have now detailed, it was not inattentive to the movements of the celestial bodies, on which he was destined to throw such a brilliant light. The imperfections of his waterclock had probably directed his thoughts to the more accurate measure of time which the motion of the sun afforded. In the yard of the house where he lived, he traced the varying movements of that luminary upon the walls and roofs of the buildings, and by means of fixed pins he had marked out the hourly and half-hourly subdivisions. One of these dials, which went by the name of Isaac’s dial, and was often referred to by the country people for the hour of the day, appears to have been drawn solely from the observations of several years; but we are not informed whether all the dials which he drew on the wall of his house at Woolsthorpe, and which existed after his death, were of the same description, or were projected from his knowledge of the doctrine of the sphere.

brewster-0006.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0006.text: Upon the death of the Reverend Mr. Smith in the year 1656, his widow left the rectory of North Witham, and took up her residence at Woolsthorpe along with her three children, Mary, Benjamin, and Hannah Smith. Newton had now attained the fifteenth year of his age, and had made great progress in his studies; and as he was thought capable of being useful in the management of the farm and country business at Woolsthorpe, his mother, chiefly from a motive of economy, recalled him from the school at Grantham. In order to accustom him to the art of selling and buying, two of the most important branches of rural labour, he was frequently sent on Saturday to Grantham market to dispose of grain and other articles of farm produce, and to purchase such necessaries as the family required. As he had yet acquired no experience, an old trustworthy servant generally accompanied him on these errands. The inn which they patronised was the Saracen’s Head at West Gate; but no sooner had they put up their horses than our young philosopher deserted his commercial concerns, and betook himself to his former lodging in the apothecary’s garret, where a number of Mr. Clark’s old books afforded him abundance of entertainment till his aged guardian had executed the family commissions, and announced to him the necessity of returning. At other times he deserted his duties at an earlier stage, and intrenched himself under a hedge by the way-side, where he continued his studies till the servant returned from Grantham. The more immediate affairs of the farm were not more prosperous under his management than would have been his marketings at Grantham. The perusal of a book, the execution of a model, or the superintendence of a waterwheel of his own construction, whirling the glittering spray from some neighbouring stream, absorbed all his thoughts when the sheep were going astray, and the cattle were devouring or treading down the corn.

brewster-0007.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0007.text: Mrs. Smith was soon convinced from experience that her son was not destined to cultivate the soil, and as his passion for study, and his dislike for every other occupation increased with his years, she wisely resolved to give him all the advantages which education could confer. He was accordingly sent back to Grantham school, where he continued for some months in busy preparation for his academical studies. His uncle, the Reverend W. Ayscough, who was rector of Burton Coggles, about three miles east of Woolsthorpe, and who had himself studied at Trinity College, recommended to his nephew to enter that society, and it was accordingly determined that he should proceed to Cambridge at the approaching term.

brewster-0009.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0009.text: When Newton, therefore, arrived at Trinity College, he brought with him a more slender portion of science than falls to the lot of ordinary scholars; but this state of his acquirements was perhaps not unfavourable to the development of his powers. Unexhausted by premature growth, and invigorated by healthful repose, his mind was the better fitted to make those vigorous and rapid shoots which soon covered with foliage and with fruit the genial soil to which it had been transferred. Cambridge was consequently the real birthplace of Newton’s genius. Her teachers fostered his earliest studies;—her institutions sustained his mightiest efforts;—and within her precincts were all his discoveries made and perfected. When he was called to higher official functions, his disciples kept up the pre-eminence of their master’s philosophy, and their successors have maintained this seat of learning in the fulness of its glory, and rendered it the most distinguished among the universities of Europe. It was on the 5th of June, 1660, in the 18th year of his age, that Newton was admitted into Trinity College, Cambridge, during the same year that Dr. Barrow was elected professor of Greek in the university. His attention was first turned to the study of mathematics by a desire to inquire into the truth of judicial astrology; and he is said to have discovered the folly of that study by erecting a figure with the aid of one or two of the problems of Euclid. The propositions contained in this ancient system of geometry he regarded as self-evident truths; and without any preliminary study he made himself master of Descartes’s Geometry by his genius and patient application. This neglect of the elementary truths of geometry he afterward regarded as a mistake in his mathematical studies, and he expressed to Dr. Pemberton his regret that “he had applied himself to the works of Descartes, and other algebraic writers, before he had considered the elements of Euclid with that attention which so excellent a writer deserved. Dr. Wallis’s Arithmetic of Infinites, Saunderson’s Logic, and the Optics of Kepler were among the books which he had studied with care. On these works he wrote comments during their perusal; and so great was his progress, that he is reported to have found himself more deeply versed in some branches of knowledge than the tutor who directed his studies.

brewster-0010.title: The Life of Sir Isaac Newton, by David Brewster
brewster-0010.text: Neither history nor tradition has handed down to us any particular account of his progress during the first three years that he spent at Cambridge. It appears from a statement of his expenses, that in 1664 he purchased a prism, for the purpose, as has been said, of examining Descartes’s theory of colours; and it is stated by Mr. Conduit, that he soon established his own views on the subject, and detected the errors in those of the French philosopher. This, however, does not seem to have been the case.
